newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Hani killer recalls S.African far-right coup plan.
newsitem.headline: Hani killer recalls S.African far-right coup plan.

text.p: South Africans on Wednesday relived the vivid danger of an armed rightwing uprising in the words of a man who almost single-handedly turned it into reality in 1993.

Clive Derby-Lewis, who killed Communist Party leader and popular hero Chris Hani in a crime that almost destroyed the transition from apartheid, said he was swamped with congratulations after the killing.

"I couldn't reply to the volume of letters I received," he told the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which is hearing amnesty applications from him and his accomplice Polish immigrant Janusz Walus, both serving life in prison.

Speaking for the first time about the murder that rocked South Africa, Derby-Lewis said he had plotted it with Walus, who gunned Hani down outside his home, to create chaos and spark a rightwing coup to ensure the survival of white rule.
"The political climate was building up to a real crescendo," he said, recalling that some 4,000 political deaths had scarred 1993, more than any year before.

He said he had carried out the killing after his party leaders and other right-wingers had repeatedly threatened to take up arms to ensure freedom for the Afrikaner volk rather than accept a South Africa ruled by blacks and Communists.

Derby-Lewis said his party, which was founded to oppose the ruling whites-only National Party's gradual rapprochement with the black majority, had never condemned him for the killing and instead provided moral and financial support.
He read at length from statements made in the months before the killing by rightwingers, such as Conservative Party leader Ferdi Hartzenberg, to show there had been a climate of war.

"We will mobilise whites. We will do everything to secure the freedom of our people. There will be no peace without their freedom. The ANC is a surrogate of world Communists," he quoted Hartzenberg as saying.
Hani's family is fiercely opposing amnesty for the two on the grounds they have failed to tell the whole truth.
The committee, due to sit for two weeks and rule later this year, has the right to grant amnesty to people who fully disclose their crime and who can prove political motives.

Derby-Lewis, a stocky 61-year-old, says Hani -- the former leader of the African National Congress armed wing who many saw as a potential successor to Nelson Mandela as president -- was a legitimate military target.
He said he himself was a target to the ANC, which could hardly argue that Hani, given his position of power, was an untouchable.
"I had at least two notable attempts on my life," he said.
